title: Why shanti three times
word: then two weeks of the peace chants
hookLine: why peace, three times? and a neighbor's blessing that also ends on peace
carry: shanti three times: within, from others, from beyond
tomorrow: take the full away from the full. what's left?

cards: Group chats end in all sorts of ways: a thumbs-up, a heart, three goodnights from the same aunt. The peace chants end with one word said three times: Om, shanti, shanti, shanti. Once would be polite.
Twice would be firm. Three times is almost a knock at the door. So, one question for today: why say peace three times?

teach.b: The tradition's answer: each shanti faces a different kind of trouble. The first is trouble from within: the body, the mind, a fever, a restless head at night. Its Sanskrit name is adhyatmika.
The second is trouble from other beings, people and animals: adhibhautika. The third is trouble from forces no one controls, storms and floods: adhidaivika.
So the ending moves outward, ring by ring: peace inside, peace with those around, peace with a world no one can steer.
That's why Hindus say it three times at the end of prayers, readings and even a ceremony at home: each shanti is sent somewhere different. A neighbor tradition ends a blessing on peace too.

In the book of Numbers, Aaron and his sons, the priests, are given words to bless the children of Israel, and the blessing closes, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace."
The Hebrew word there is shalom. What's shared: a blessing that ends by asking for peace, said over people about to go back into their lives.
What's honestly different: the priestly blessing asks peace from the LORD's face turned toward the people, spoken by the priests over them.

The threefold shanti, in the reading taught here, names three directions trouble comes from, and teacher and student say it together. Two blessings, each in its own words, each ending where people need it.

how: Hindus close the peace chants, and many prayers and readings, with Om shanti shanti shanti; teachers often explain the three as peace from troubles within, from other beings, and from forces beyond control.

games.q: what does “then two weeks of the peace chants” mean?
o: war songs sung before two armies meet
chants that end with peace, said three times
a vow of silence before entering a temple

games.q: three shantis, three troubles. tap the pairs.
p: trouble from forces no one controls

s: the three shantis are the same word repeated for emphasis
in the traditional reading, each faces a different trouble: within, from others, from beyond.
a blessing in the book of Numbers also ends by asking for peace
"The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." (Numbers 6:26, JPS 1917)
blessings in every religion are really the same blessing
each has its own words and setting: the priestly blessing and the shanti share an ending on peace and differ in who asks, and how.

games.q: your Jewish friend's family hears a blessing that ends 'and give thee peace'; your chants end with shanti three times. what's a fair way to put it?
o: shalom and shanti are one word that the two traditions borrowed from each other.
they're the same prayer, just said in two languages.
both end on peace; one asks it from God's face, one names three troubles.
games.why: a real shared thing, an ending on peace, and a real difference in who blesses and what is named. neither needs to become the other.

practice: Listen in three rings. First, a sound inside you: your breath, your heartbeat. Then a sound in the room, and last, one from outside, a car, the wind, a bird, giving each ring its own stretch of the sit.

wordCard.voice: The peace chants end in shanti, three times: peace within, peace with others, peace with forces no one controls.

orig.note: Sanskrit: peace; said three times to close the peace chants.

carryVoice: Keep this one: shanti three times, peace within, from others, and from beyond. None left out. Shanti.
